a: my grandfather Jesus
p: The translator is the author's grandson; the author is Jesus (Yeshua), whom the book's end calls son of Sirach.
b: The prologue is the only part of the book written in Greek from the start. Its writer never gives his own name, only that he is the grandson of the author. The grandfather is Iēsous, the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua (Joshua), the same name as Jesus of Nazareth. Near the end of the book he signs his work: "I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem" (50:27). From "son of Sirach" come the names Sirach (Greek) and Ben Sira (Hebrew). The prologue shows a family tradition of learning: the grandfather studied the Scriptures and wrote, and the grandson carried his book to a new land and language.
orig: ὁ πάππος μου Ἰησοῦς (ho pappos mou Iēsous), 'my grandfather Jesus'

a: the law and the prophets and the others who came after them
t: The law, the prophets and the other books
p: Three times the grandson names three groups of books. Is this the Bible's three-part shape already, or a looser list?
b: The grandson names Israel's books three times: "the law and the prophets and the others who came after them," "the law, the prophets and the other books of our ancestors," and "the law itself, the prophecies and the rest of the books." The Jewish Bible still has three parts: Torah (law), Nevi'im (prophets) and Ketuvim (writings). This prologue is generally counted as the earliest witness to that three-part shape. Readers differ on how much it proves. Some take the third group as already a known, fixed collection. Others point out that the grandson never gives it a name: he calls it only "the others" or "the rest," which may mean the third group was still open. Compare Jesus' words in Luke 24:44, "in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms."
l: Development of the Hebrew Bible canon
Development of the Hebrew Bible canon

a: praised for instruction and wisdom
p: Paideia means upbringing and education: here "instruction," and "discipline" only where it hurts (4:17).
b: The grandson pairs two words twice: paideia and sophia, "instruction and wisdom." Paideia was the Greek word for a child's whole upbringing: schooling, training and correction. It translates the Hebrew musar, which Proverbs' Plain gives as "discipline" (Proverbs 1:2, 7). In this part of Sirach the Plain uses "instruction" where the sense is learning (here, 1:27, 4:24, 6:18) and "discipline" where Wisdom corrects and tests a learner (4:17). A Greek reader in Egypt would hear in the prologue the language of the schools: the Jewish Scriptures offer a paideia as good as any Greek one.
orig: παιδεία καὶ σοφία (paideia kai sophia)

a: Words spoken in Hebrew do not carry the same force
p: The grandson warns that a translation never says quite what the original says, even for the law and the prophets.
b: This is one of the earliest comments anyone made on translating the Bible. The verb isodynamei means "have equal power": Hebrew words lose force in Greek. The grandson adds that the same is true of "the law itself, the prophecies and the rest of the books," which shows that Greek translations of those books already existed in his day, the beginnings of what we call the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament made before Jesus. His warning applies to his own work too. Where the Hebrew of Ben Sira survives, it often differs from his Greek, and this site gives those differences in its variant notes.
orig: οὐ γὰρ ἰσοδυναμεῖ (ou gar isodynamei), 'for they do not have equal force'

a: the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes
t: When the grandson came to Egypt
p: Euergetes is taken to be Ptolemy VIII, so the grandson reached Egypt in 132 BC.
b: Euergetes, "Benefactor," was a title of Egypt's Greek kings, the Ptolemies. Most scholars take this to be Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, which puts the grandson's arrival in Egypt in 132 BC. The grandfather would then have written in Jerusalem a generation or two before, usually dated about 180 BC, before the crisis under Antiochus IV that 1 Maccabees tells. The Greek synchronisas, "having spent time," says that the grandson lived in Egypt some while before he finished the translation.
orig: ἐν τῷ ὀγδόῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἔτει ἐπὶ τοῦ Εὐεργέτου βασιλέως

a: I found a copy that held no small instruction
t: What did he find in Egypt?
p: The rare word aphomoion probably means "a copy" of the book; it can also be read as "no small difference" in learning.
b: The Greek aphomoion is rare. It means something made to look like another thing: a likeness or a copy. Read that way, the grandson found in Egypt a copy of his grandfather's book, which held no small instruction, and this moved him to translate it (the KJV has "a book of no small learning"). Another reading takes the phrase as "no small difference (or likeness) of education": he found the level of learning among Egypt's Jews to be such that a translation was needed. The Plain follows the first reading, which fits the next sentence, "translating this book."
orig: εὗρον οὐ μικρᾶς παιδείας ἀφόμοιον (heuron ou mikras paideias aphomoion)

a: those living as foreigners in other lands
p: The grandson writes for the Jews of the dispersion, especially in Egypt, who read their Scriptures in Greek.
b: The Greek paroikia means living somewhere as a resident foreigner. By the 100s BC large Jewish communities lived in Egypt, above all in Alexandria, and spoke Greek. The grandson wants them to have his grandfather's teaching so that they can "live by the law" far from Jerusalem. The same word family appears in 1 Peter, which calls Christians "resident aliens" (1 Peter 1:17) and writes to "temporary residents of the Dispersion" (1 Peter 1:1).
orig: τοῖς ἐν τῇ παροικίᾳ (tois en tē paroikia)

a: All wisdom comes from the Lord
p: Ben Sira opens where Proverbs and James agree: wisdom is God's gift before it is a human skill.
b: The whole book rests on this line. Wisdom is not first a human achievement or a school subject; it belongs to God and comes from him. "It is the LORD who gives wisdom" (Proverbs 2:6), and James tells anyone who lacks it to "ask God for it" (James 1:5). In Greek Sirach, "Lord" (Kyrios) stands for God's name, so the Plain writes "the Lord," not "the LORD." The Catholic lectionary reads 1:1–10 at Mass on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time.

a: Who will trace out
p: The verb means to follow a trail; Paul uses its opposite of God's ways (Romans 11:33).
b: Exichniazō comes from ichnos, a footprint: to track something down by its prints. Ben Sira lists things no one can measure, the sky, the earth, the deep, and then adds wisdom. Job 28 asks the same question ("But wisdom: where can it be found?" Job 28:12), and so does Baruch 3:29. Paul uses a related word when he praises God's wisdom: no one can "follow the tracks of his ways" (Romans 11:33, Greek anexichniastoi).
orig: τίς ἐξιχνιάσει; (tis exichniasei), 'who will track it out?'

a: Wisdom was created first of all things
p: As in Proverbs 8:22, Wisdom is created first; Christians later argued over what such words mean for Christ.
b: Here Wisdom begins to act like a person, so the Plain gives her a capital W (as Proverbs does for Lady Wisdom). The verb ektistai, "has been created," matches the Greek of Proverbs 8:22, where Wisdom says the LORD made her first of his works (the Hebrew there is "acquired me"). For Ben Sira, Wisdom is God's first creature, not a second god. Christians read such passages of Christ, "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), and in the 300s Arius and his opponents argued over whether "created" could be said of the Son. Most churches answered with the Nicene Creed: the Son is "begotten, not made." Jewish readers identify Wisdom with the Torah, as Ben Sira himself does in 24:23.
orig: προτέρα πάντων ἔκτισται σοφία (protera pantōn ektistai sophia)

a: her clever plans
p: The Greek word usually means cunning; here it is Wisdom's skill, like Proverbs' "shrewdness" in the good sense.
b: Panourgeuma comes from panourgos, "able to do anything," which in Greek is often bad: crafty, sly. The Septuagint also uses it in a good sense for the shrewdness Proverbs praises (Proverbs 1:4; 8:5). Ben Sira uses the word of Wisdom's own clever ways, which only God fully knows. In 6:32 the learner who gives himself to her becomes panourgos, "shrewd."
orig: τὰ πανουργεύματα αὐτῆς (ta panourgeumata autēs)

a: Only one is wise
p: God alone is wise in himself, seated as king; the New Testament praises "the only wise God."
b: Wisdom belongs fully to God alone, the king on his throne (Isaiah 6:1; Psalm 47:8). People may become wise, but only by receiving it. The New Testament uses the same idea in praise: "to the only wise God" (Romans 16:27). The Latin Bible expands the verse into a longer praise of "the most high Creator Almighty" (Vulgate 1:8), which the Douay-Rheims translates.

a: poured her out over all his works
t: Wisdom poured out, and the Latin "in the Holy Spirit"
p: God shares Wisdom with creation like poured liquid; the Latin adds that he created her "in the Holy Spirit."
b: The image is generous: Wisdom is poured over everything God made, so the order of the world shows her (Proverbs 3:19; Psalm 104:24). The same verb is used for God pouring out his Spirit (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). The Latin Vulgate, which Catholic Bibles followed for centuries, reads "He created her in the Holy Spirit" (Vulgate 1:9; Douay: "in the Holy Ghost"), a phrase not in the Greek or the KJV. Catholic and Orthodox readers have often heard in this chapter the Father, his Wisdom (the Son) and the Spirit together; Jewish readers and many scholars read it of God and his created Wisdom only.
orig: ἐξέχεεν αὐτήν (execheen autēn), 'he poured her out'

a: to those who love him
t: Wisdom for everyone, and more for those who love God
p: All people get a share of wisdom; those who love God get her in full.
b: Ben Sira makes two claims at once. Every human being ("all flesh") has some wisdom, as much as God gives. But God "supplied her freely," in rich measure, to those who love him. The phrase "those who love him" is the Bible's language for the covenant people (Exodus 20:6; Deuteronomy 7:9). James promises "the crown of life" to those who love God (James 1:12), and Paul speaks of what God has prepared "for those who love him" (1 Corinthians 2:9). In 24:8 Ben Sira will say where Wisdom found her home: in Israel.

a: The fear of the Lord
p: Ben Sira's key phrase: the awe, reverence and obedience that Proverbs calls the start of wisdom.
b: This phrase runs through the book more than any other. The Greek phobos Kyriou renders the Hebrew yir'at YHWH, which Proverbs' Plain gives as "the fear of the LORD" (Proverbs 1:7). Because the Greek has no divine name, the Plain here has "the Lord." The "fear" is not panic. It is the respect of a creature before the Creator, which shows itself in obedience and trust. Ben Sira can say in one breath that it brings "gladness and a garland of joy" (1:11) and that it is the root of wisdom (1:20). Chapter 1 is a small hymn to it: 1:11–20 names it again and again.
orig: φόβος Κυρίου (phobos Kyriou)

a: on the day his life ends
t: "At the last": the end of life
p: Ben Sira means a good end to this life; he does not teach a resurrection, as later Jewish and Christian readers would.
b: "At the last" (ep' eschatōn) and "the day of his end" mean the close of a person's life: a peaceful death, an honored name and children who carry on. Ben Sira does not speak here of judgment after death or of rising again; elsewhere he says plainly that the dead do not praise God (17:27–28), and his book has no hope of resurrection. In this he stands with much of the Hebrew Bible (Psalm 6:5) and goes less far than Daniel 12:2 or the Wisdom of Solomon 3:1–9. Christian readers in the churches that keep the book often hear "the last" as the last judgment, a fuller meaning the New Testament supplies.
r: 17:27–28; Psalm 6:5; Daniel 12:2; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1–9; Proverbs 23:18

a: The start of wisdom is to fear God
p: Ben Sira repeats Proverbs' motto, then adds that Wisdom was formed with the faithful in the womb.
b: This is the motto of Israel's wisdom books: "The start of wisdom is the fear of the LORD" (Proverbs 9:10; compare Proverbs 1:7; Psalm 111:10; Job 28:28). Ben Sira then adds his own image: Wisdom was "formed along with the faithful while they were in the womb." As Jeremiah was known before he was shaped in the belly (Jeremiah 1:5), the faithful are given Wisdom from the start of life. The "faithful" (pistoi) are the people who keep faith with God, Israel at its best.
r: Proverbs 9:10; Proverbs 1:7; Psalm 111:10; Job 28:28; Jeremiah 1:5; Psalm 22:10

a: she built her nest
p: The Greek verb is a bird's word: Wisdom nests among people, an early hint of her "tent" in Israel (24:8).
b: Enosseusen comes from neossos, a nestling: she "made her nest." The picture is homely and warm. Wisdom, who was with God before everything (1:4), settles among human beings like a bird building where it means to stay, and she will be "entrusted" to their children. Chapter 24 takes the idea further: Wisdom searches for a resting place and pitches her tent in Jacob (24:7–8), language that John 1:14 echoes when the Word "pitched his tent" among us.
orig: ἐνόσσευσεν (enosseusen), 'she nested'

a: until they are drunk with it
p: Wisdom feeds people so well that they are "drunk": a picture of joy, as at Wisdom's banquet in Proverbs 9.
b: Methyskei means "makes drunk." Ben Sira uses it boldly for the fullness of joy that the fear of the Lord brings. Proverbs pictures Wisdom setting a table and calling, "Come, have some of my bread, / and drink the wine I mixed" (Proverbs 9:5). Isaiah invites the thirsty to wine and milk without price (Isaiah 55:1). The next verse turns from the feast to the farm: Wisdom fills house and barns.
orig: μεθύσκει αὐτούς (methyskei autous)
r: Proverbs 9:1–6; Proverbs 9:5; Isaiah 55:1; Song of Songs 5:1; 24:19–21

a: Wisdom's root
p: Root and branches: Wisdom is a living tree whose root is the fear of the Lord and whose branches are long life.
b: In 1:6 Ben Sira asked who knows Wisdom's root; now he answers: the fear of the Lord. Proverbs also calls Wisdom a tree: "To those who grab hold of her she is a tree of life" (Proverbs 3:18). The image prepares for chapter 24, where Wisdom grows like a cedar, a palm and a vine (24:13–17). The righteous person, too, is a well-watered tree (Psalm 1:3), while 6:3 warns of a man who leaves himself "like dry wood."

a: can never be declared right
p: The verb is "be justified," a law-court word: a man ruled by unjust anger will never be acquitted.
b: Dikaiōthēnai, "to be justified," is the verb Paul uses for God's verdict on the sinner (Romans 3:24). Here it has its plain courtroom sense: to be found in the right. Anger that is unjust will never win that verdict, because "the swing" (rhopē, the tipping of a scale) of a man's anger brings him down. James makes a similar point: "a man's anger does not bring about God's righteousness" (James 1:20).
orig: οὐ δυνήσεται θυμὸς ἄδικος δικαιωθῆναι

a: a sinner loathes reverence for God
p: The word bdelygma (KJV "abomination") is turned around: the sinner finds devotion to God disgusting.
b: Bdelygma is the Septuagint's word for the Hebrew to'evah, what is abhorrent, often what God hates. Ben Sira turns it around: to a sinner, theosebeia, reverence for God, is the abhorrent thing. Proverbs makes the same point from both sides: "the wicked find a man who walks straight abhorrent" (Proverbs 29:27).
orig: βδέλυγμα δὲ ἁμαρτωλῷ θεοσέβεια (bdelygma de hamartōlō theosebeia)

a: Keep the commandments
p: Ben Sira's great joining: whoever wants wisdom must keep the law of Moses.
b: Earlier wisdom books said little about Moses' law. Ben Sira joins the two firmly. Wisdom is God's gift, and the way to receive it is to keep the commandments. He will say outright that all Wisdom's praise is "the book of the covenant of God Most High" (24:23), the law of Moses. Deuteronomy had already said that keeping the law would be Israel's wisdom in the eyes of the nations (Deuteronomy 4:6). Jewish tradition kept this joining of Torah and wisdom; Christians read it alongside Jesus' call to keep his commandments (John 14:15) and Paul's teaching on law and grace.

a: his delight is faith and gentleness
p: Pistis is faith and faithfulness; praotēs is gentleness, the word Jesus uses of himself.
b: Pistis in Ben Sira means trust in God and the faithfulness that goes with it (2:6–10). Praotēs is gentleness, the opposite of harshness and pride (3:17; 4:8). Jesus calls himself "gentle" (praus) in Matthew 11:29, in a saying that also echoes Ben Sira's picture of Wisdom's yoke (6:24–30). Paul lists faithfulness and gentleness among the Spirit's fruit (Galatians 5:22–23).
orig: πίστις καὶ πρᾳότης (pistis kai praotēs)

a: a double heart
p: A "double" or divided heart is one that serves God and something else; James calls such a person "double-minded."
b: Kardia dissē, "a double heart," renders a Hebrew idiom, lev valev, "a heart and a heart," which Psalm 12:2 uses of liars: "with a divided heart." Ben Sira returns to the theme several times in this part: the sinner on "two paths" (2:12) and the "sinner who has two tongues" (5:9; 6:1). James warns against the dipsychos, the "double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:8).
orig: ἐν καρδίᾳ δισσῇ (en kardia dissē)

a: put on an act
p: Hypokrinomai means to play a part on stage; from it comes "hypocrite."
b: A Greek hypokritēs was a stage actor. Ben Sira's verb means to play a part "in the mouths of people," that is, to act out a piety that wins people's talk and praise. Jesus uses the same word family of those who give, pray and fast "to win praise from people" (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16).
orig: μὴ ὑποκριθῇς ἐν στόμασιν ἀνθρώπων (mē hypokrithēs en stomasin anthrōpōn)

a: throw you down in the middle of the assembly
p: The proud man's secret sins come out in front of the community gathering, the worst shame a Jerusalem man could suffer.
b: Synagōgē, "gathering, assembly," is the word later used for the synagogue, but here it is the assembled community of Jerusalem, where cases were judged and reputations made or lost. Proverbs' young man laments that he "very nearly came to complete disaster / in the middle of the assembly and the community" (Proverbs 5:14). Ben Sira's warning matches Jesus' words: "everyone who raises himself up will be brought low" (Luke 14:11).
orig: ἐν μέσῳ συναγωγῆς (en mesō synagōgēs)

a: My child
p: Ben Sira speaks as a teacher to a pupil; where his Hebrew survives, it has "my son."
b: The Greek teknon means "child." Ben Sira uses it as a teacher's address to his pupil, as Proverbs does ("My son," Proverbs 1:8). Where the Hebrew of this part survives, from 3:8 on, it has beni, "my son" (for example 3:12, 3:17 and 4:1, where the Greek has teknon). The pupils of a Jerusalem school were young men, so "my son" was literal in its way. The grandson's Greek "my child" makes the teaching open to any reader, which suits how Jews and Christians have used the book since.
orig: Τέκνον (teknon), 'child'; Hebrew בני (beni), 'my son'

a: make your soul ready for testing
p: Whoever sets out to serve God should expect to be tested; James and 1 Peter say the same.
b: Peirasmos means testing or trial (the same word can mean temptation). Ben Sira tells the beginner not to be surprised by hardship: it comes with serving God, as Abraham was tested (Genesis 22:1). The New Testament says the same in words close to these: "My brothers, when you fall into all sorts of trials, treat it as complete joy" (James 1:2), and 1 Peter 1:6–7 speaks of faith proved by fire (compare 2:5). The Catholic lectionary reads 2:1–11 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time.
r: Genesis 22:1; James 1:2–4; James 1:12; 1 Peter 1:6–7; 2 Timothy 3:12; Matthew 6:13

a: Fire is where gold is proved
p: As gold is refined by fire, people God accepts are proved by humiliation.
b: Metal-workers heated gold in a furnace to burn off what was not gold. The Bible often uses the picture: "Silver goes in the melting pot and gold in the furnace, / but it is the LORD who puts hearts to the test" (Proverbs 17:3; compare Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3). The Wisdom of Solomon says of the righteous, "He proved them like gold in a smelter's fire" (Wisdom of Solomon 3:6), and 1 Peter 1:7 calls faith worth more than gold that "fire tests." Ben Sira's furnace is tapeinōsis, being made low: loss, shame and poverty.
orig: ἐν καμίνῳ ταπεινώσεως (en kaminō tapeinōseōs)
r: Proverbs 17:3; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3; Wisdom of Solomon 3:6; 1 Peter 1:7; Job 23:10

a: you who fear the Lord
p: Three lines say "you who fear the Lord" (2:7–9), three more "those who fear the Lord" (2:15–17).
b: Ben Sira writes for a school, and repetition helps students learn by heart. Here three commands to "you who fear the Lord" (wait, believe, hope) are answered later by three promises about "those who fear the Lord" (2:15–17). The Plain keeps the same English each time. The Latin Vulgate adds a fourth line: "you that fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened" (Vulgate 2:10, Douay), which is not in the Greek or the KJV.

a: Look back at the ancient generations and see
p: Ben Sira appeals to Israel's past: no one who trusted God was finally put to shame.
b: Ben Sira's proof is history. Psalm 22 makes the same appeal: "They called to you and escaped; / they trusted you and were never shamed" (Psalm 22:5). Paul cites Isaiah 28:16 for the same promise (Romans 10:11). Ben Sira will later spend seven chapters on "the ancient generations" in his Praise of the Fathers (44–50). Some readers find the claim too simple next to Job or the Psalms of lament; Ben Sira's answer is in 2:4–5: hardship is real, but it is testing, not abandonment.

a: he forgives sins
p: Ben Sira echoes God's self-description to Moses; James 5:11 uses the same pair of ideas.
b: This is the creed of Israel, first spoken to Moses: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6; compare Psalm 103:8). Ben Sira uses two Greek words, oiktirmōn ("full of pity") and eleēmōn ("merciful"). James, after pointing to Job's endurance, ends with "for the Lord is very tender-hearted and compassionate" (James 5:11), using oiktirmōn too. Whether James knew Ben Sira, or both simply draw on Exodus 34:6, these words alone cannot settle.
orig: οἰκτείρμων καὶ ἐλεήμων (oikteirmōn kai eleēmōn)

a: the sinner who steps onto two paths
p: The sinner tries to walk two roads: God's and his own.
b: The Bible often pictures life as two ways, one leading to life and one to death (Psalm 1:6; Deuteronomy 30:15; Matthew 7:13–14). Ben Sira's sinner tries to have both. Elijah asked Israel, "How long will you limp between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21), and Jesus said, "No one can be a slave to two masters" (Matthew 6:24). Compare the "double heart" of 1:28.

a: when the Lord pays his visit
p: Episkeptomai, "visit," means God coming to inspect: to rescue or to judge.
b: In the Greek Bible God's "visit" can be good news (he visited Sarah, Genesis 21:1; he visited his people to redeem them, Luke 1:68) or bad news (he will visit sin, Exodus 32:34). Here it is the day of reckoning, when those who gave up will have nothing to show. Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it "did not know the time of its visitation" (Luke 19:44).
orig: ὅταν ἐπισκέπτηται ὁ κύριος (hotan episkeptētai ho kyrios)

a: filled full of the law
t: Love that is filled with the law
p: For Ben Sira, loving God and loving his law are one thing.
b: Those who love God are "filled" with the law, the way the earlier verses spoke of being filled with Wisdom's fruit (1:16–17). For Ben Sira the law is not a burden laid on unwilling people but the food of those who love God. The psalmist speaks the same way: "the law of the LORD is his delight" (Psalm 1:2; compare Psalm 119:97). Jesus joined love and obedience too: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments" (John 14:15).

a: We will fall into the Lord's hands
t: Better God's hands than human hands
p: Ben Sira takes up David's choice in 2 Samuel 24: better to fall into God's hands, for his mercy is as great as he is.
b: When David had to choose a punishment, he said, "let us fall into the LORD's hand, for his compassion runs deep. Into a human hand, let me not fall" (2 Samuel 24:14; 1 Chronicles 21:13). Ben Sira makes David's words a rule for all who fear the Lord. Hebrews uses the same picture as a warning: "Falling into the hands of the living God is a terrifying thing" (Hebrews 10:31). Both are true for Ben Sira, who sets mercy and anger side by side (5:6). The Latin adds "If we do not do penance" before the line (Vulgate 2:22, Douay), a phrase Catholic preaching has used.

a: Hear me, children, for I am your father
t: A teacher speaks as a father
p: Ben Sira addresses his pupils as "children" and himself as their "father," as teachers in Israel did.
b: In Israel's schools the teacher was called "father" and his pupils "sons" (Proverbs 4:1; 2 Kings 2:12, where Elisha calls Elijah "my father"). So Ben Sira's first lesson on honoring fathers and mothers is spoken by a teacher who is himself a kind of father. The promise "so that you will be kept safe" (sōthēte, literally "be saved") means a safe and good life, the reward Exodus 20:12 attaches to honoring parents.

a: makes atonement for sins
p: The Ten Commandments promise long life to those who honor parents; Ben Sira adds that it atones for sins.
b: The fifth commandment promises "so that your days will stretch out long" (Exodus 20:12). Ben Sira keeps that promise (3:6) but goes beyond it: the one who honors a father "makes atonement for sins" (exilasetai, the Greek Bible's word for the Hebrew kipper), and kindness to a father is set "in place of" sins (3:14). The Hebrew of 3:3 is lost (the Cairo manuscript begins at 3:6). Catholic teaching quotes 3:2–6, 12–13 and 16 on the duties of grown children (Catechism 2218). Protestant readers, for whom the book is not Scripture, hold that sins are atoned for only by Christ's sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10–14), and read Ben Sira as saying that God looks kindly on the dutiful child. For the parallel claim about alms, see 3:30.
orig: ὁ τιμῶν πατέρα ἐξιλάσεται ἁμαρτίας (ho timōn patera exilasetai hamartias)

a: will have a long life
p: Long life is the promise of the fifth commandment, "the first commandment that comes with a promise."
b: "Honor your father and your mother, so that your days will stretch out long on the land the LORD your God is giving you" (Exodus 20:12). Ben Sira's whole passage (3:1–16) is a sermon on this one commandment. Paul quotes it to Christian children: "This is the first commandment that comes with a promise" (Ephesians 6:2). Jesus defended it against a custom that let a son vow his support money to God instead (Mark 7:10–13). The Catholic lectionary reads 3:2–6 and 3:12–14 on the Feast of the Holy Family.

a: In what you do and in what you say
t: The Hebrew: "all blessings will overtake you"
p: From here the Hebrew survives: "My son, in word and deed honor your father, so that all blessings may overtake you."
b: The Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863) begins in the middle of 3:6 and has this verse as "My son, in word and in deed honor your father, so that all blessings may overtake you." The last words echo Deuteronomy 28:2: "All these blessings will come on you and catch up with you." The Greek has a single "blessing from him" and no "my son."
orig: בני במאמר ובמעשה כבד אביך עבור ישיגוך כל ברכות

a: A father's blessing
p: A parent's blessing or curse was believed to shape the children's future; the Hebrew pictures roots and plants.
b: Israel's stories turn on a father's blessing: Isaac's over Jacob and Esau (Genesis 27), Jacob's over his sons (Genesis 49). A parent's words were believed to carry real power. The Greek speaks of houses and foundations. The Hebrew of manuscript A uses a garden picture instead: "a father's blessing lays down a root, but a mother's curse tears up what is planted."
orig: ברכת אב תיסד שרש וקללת אם תנתש נטע

a: support your father in his old age
p: Ben Sira turns to grown children: the commandment means caring for parents when they are old and weak.
b: Honoring parents is not only for small children. Ben Sira speaks to grown sons whose fathers are old: help him, be patient if his mind fails, do not shame him. Proverbs says the same: "Do not look down on your mother because she has grown old" (Proverbs 23:22). 1 Timothy 5:4 tells children and grandchildren to repay their parents. The Hebrew here reads "My son, be strong in honoring your father, and do not leave him all the days of your life." The Catholic Catechism quotes 3:12–13 on the support that grown children owe their parents in old age and illness (2218).

a: if his understanding fades
p: Ben Sira foresees an aging father losing his wits, and asks the son for patience, not contempt.
b: Apoleipē synesin, "if he lacks understanding," describes an old man whose mind is going. The son is to "have pardon" (syngnōmēn eche, the same phrase the grandson uses in the prologue when he asks readers to pardon his translation). The last line, "in all your strength," may mean "while you are strong and he is weak" or "with all your might, do not shame him"; the Plain takes the first. The Hebrew has "even if his mind fails, leave him be, and do not shame him all the days of his life."
orig: κἂν ἀπολείπῃ σύνεσιν, συγγνώμην ἔχε (kan apoleipē synesin, syngnōmēn eche)

a: Mercy shown to a father
t: "Mercy" to a father: the word for alms
p: The Greek word is eleēmosynē, the word for alms; the Hebrew is tsedaqah. Both reappear in 3:30.
b: Eleēmosynē means an act of mercy, and in the Greek Bible it came to mean alms, gifts to the poor (Tobit 4:7–11). Here it is the kindness a son shows his father. The Hebrew has tsidqat av, the "righteousness" (or charity) shown to a father. In Hebrew of this period tsedaqah could mean both doing right and giving to the poor. The same pair, Greek eleēmosynē and Hebrew tsedaqah, stands in 3:30. Where the Greek says this kindness "will be built up as a house," the Hebrew says it "will be planted" in place of sin.
orig: ἐλεημοσύνη πατρός (eleēmosynē patros); Hebrew צדקת אב (tsidqat av)

a: As warm, clear weather does to frost
p: Sins dissolve as frost melts in the morning sun.
b: Frost was a real sight on cold winter mornings in the hills of Judea, gone as soon as the sun came out. Ben Sira uses it for how God removes sin. Isaiah used snow and wool: "If your sins are scarlet, / like snow they will turn white" (Isaiah 1:18). The Hebrew reads "like heat upon frost, to put an end to your iniquities."

a: Like someone who speaks against God
p: The Greek calls him "like a blasphemer"; the Hebrew says he acts in defiance and provokes his Creator.
b: The Greek blasphēmos is "one who speaks against God": dishonoring a father is like insulting God, who gave the father his honor (3:2). The Hebrew is stronger still: "for one who despises his father acts with defiance, and one who curses his mother provokes his Creator." The law punished cursing a parent with death: "Anyone who curses his father or his mother must be put to death" (Exodus 21:17).
orig: ὡς βλάσφημος (hōs blasphēmos); Hebrew כי מזיד בוזה אביו ומכעיס בוראו מקלל אמו

a: make yourself that much lower
p: Ben Sira's rule for the powerful: the higher you rise, the lower you should make yourself.
b: The verse is a key text on humility. Proverbs says, "the humble he gives his favor" (Proverbs 3:34), a verse quoted twice in the New Testament (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Jesus taught, "the one who brings himself low will be raised up" (Luke 14:11), and Paul urges, "Do not set your minds on lofty things, but go along with the lowly" (Romans 12:16). The Hebrew reads "Make yourself small, away from all the world's greatness, and before God you will find mercy." The Catholic lectionary reads 3:17–18, 20, 28–29 on the 22nd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C).
r: Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5; Luke 14:11; Romans 12:16; Philippians 2:3–8

a: Do not go looking for things harder than you can handle
t: Limits on searching out God's secrets
p: Do not pry into what is beyond you. The Talmud quotes these lines by name from "the book of Ben Sira."
b: The Babylonian Talmud quotes 3:21–22 in Hebrew, naming its source: "as it is written in the book of Ben Sira: Do not seek what is too wonderful for you, and do not search into what is hidden from you. Consider what you have been allowed; you have no business with hidden things" (Hagigah 13a, as the Sefaria text gives it). The rabbis used it to set limits on speculation about divine mysteries. Manuscript A has almost the same Hebrew. Psalm 131:1 says, "I have not gone walking among great things / or among wonders beyond me," and Deuteronomy 29:29, "What is hidden is for the LORD our God." Many readers hear in Ben Sira's lines a caution about the Greek learning of his day. Others take them more simply as a warning against pride in any age.
orig: Hebrew פלאות ממך אל תדרוש ומכוסה ממך אל תחקור
r: Psalm 131:1; Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 12:3; Ecclesiastes 7:23–24; Babylonian Talmud Hagigah 13a

a: more than human understanding has already been shown to you
t: Israel has already been shown more
p: Ben Sira tells his pupil he already has more than human wisdom can reach: the revelation given to Israel.
b: Why not pry into hidden things? Because, Ben Sira says, you have already been shown more than human minds can grasp. He means God's law and Israel's Scriptures (compare 24:23). Deuteronomy says the same: hidden things belong to God, "What has been made known is for us and our children" (Deuteronomy 29:29). The Hebrew of the first line reads "With what is beyond you, do not be stubborn."

a: A hard heart
p: The Greek's "hard heart" renders the Hebrew "heavy heart," the word used of Pharaoh.
b: Kardia sklēra is "a hard heart." The Hebrew behind it, in manuscript A, is lev kaved, "a heavy heart," the same word used of Pharaoh: "Pharaoh's heart is heavy. He refuses to let the people go" (Exodus 7:14). The site keeps the Hebrew words apart (stubborn, heavy, hard), but the Greek here has only "hard." A heart so weighed down cannot respond, and it "will come to harm at the end."
orig: καρδία σκληρά (kardia sklēra); Hebrew לב כבד (lev kaved)

a: turns a proverb over and over
p: Parabolē, "proverb," is the same Greek word as the Gospels' "parable."
b: Parabolē renders the Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs, riddles and stories with a point. The Gospels use parabolē for Jesus' parables. A thoughtful heart turns such sayings over, as Proverbs 1:6 says the wise do with "a proverb and a figure." The Hebrew of manuscript A reads "the heart of the wise will understand the proverbs of the wise."
orig: παραβολή (parabolē); Hebrew משלי חכמים (mishlei chakhamim)

a: A blazing fire is put out by water
p: One of the book's best-known sayings. The Greek has "alms"; the Hebrew has tsedaqah, "righteousness" or charity.
b: As surely as water puts out fire, alms put out sin. The Greek is eleēmosynē exilasetai hamartias, "alms will atone for sins." Manuscript A reads "Water puts out a blazing fire; so tsedaqah atones for sin." The Hebrew verb is kipper, the temple word for atonement, and tsedaqah is "righteousness," which in this period also meant charity to the poor. Other books say the same: "Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin" (Tobit 12:9); Daniel tells a king to break with his sins "by showing mercy to the poor" (Daniel 4:27); "Guilt is atoned for by loyal love and faithfulness" (Proverbs 16:6); "love lays a cover over a great number of sins" (1 Peter 4:8). The Didache, an early Christian manual, says, "Of whatsoever thou hast gained by thy hands thou shalt give a ransom for thy sins" (Didache 4:6, Lake's translation). Whether such giving takes away sin is a question churches answer differently; the "Where Christians differ" card at Tobit 4 sets out their answers.
orig: ἐλεημοσύνη ἐξιλάσεται ἁμαρτίας; Hebrew כן צדקה תכפר חטאת
r: Tobit 4:10; Tobit 12:9; Daniel 4:27; Proverbs 16:6; Proverbs 10:2; 1 Peter 4:8; Luke 11:41; Didache 4:6

a: eyes that look to you in need
p: Do not keep the poor waiting: the law required that a poor worker be paid the same day.
b: The poor man's "eyes" are fixed on the one who can help him; to make him wait is cruel. The law told employers, "Pay him his wages each day, before the sun goes down, because he is poor and his heart is set on it" (Deuteronomy 24:15). James warns rich landowners that the unpaid wages of their workers "cries out" (James 5:4). Ben Sira's 4:1–10 is a short code of conduct toward the poor, for pupils who would one day have money and power.

a: the one who made him will listen to his plea
t: God hears the poor man's curse
p: A poor man's bitter cry reaches his Maker; the law said the same of the oppressed widow, orphan and worker.
b: Ben Sira does not say the curse is magic; he says God listens to the one who utters it. The law warns about the orphan and the widow: "If you do treat him harshly, and he cries out to me, be sure I will hear his cry" (Exodus 22:23), and about the unpaid worker: "he will cry out to the LORD against you" (Deuteronomy 24:15). Proverbs calls oppressing the poor "taunting the one who made them" (Proverbs 14:31). The Hebrew of manuscript A calls God "his Rock" (tsuro).

a: Make the assembly fond of you
p: Ben Sira's pupils would take part in Jerusalem's public life: its assembly, its great men and its law courts.
b: The synagōgē here is the assembly of the city's citizens; the megistan is a man of high rank, an official or noble. Jerusalem in the early 100s BC was a temple city under the Seleucid kings of Syria, run by the high priest, a council of elders and leading families. Ben Sira's pupils came from families who could expect to sit in the assembly and even as judges (4:9). He teaches them to be liked, to show proper respect, and still to stand up for the wronged.

a: when you give judgment
t: The pupil as a future judge
p: Some of Ben Sira's pupils would sit as judges; he warns them not to lose their nerve when the powerful are guilty.
b: En tō krinein se, "when you judge," assumes the pupil will one day decide cases. The danger is oligopsychia, "smallness of soul": being too timid to rule against the strong. The law demanded fairness to rich and poor alike: "Do not lift up the face of the poor man, and do not honor the face of the great man" (Leviticus 19:15). The Hebrew of manuscript A reads "Rescue the oppressed from his oppressors, and do not be impatient with a just judgment."

a: you will be as a son of the Most High
t: A son of the Most High
p: Caring for orphans and widows makes a person like God, who is father to the orphan; Jesus uses the same words.
b: God himself is "a father to orphans / and a judge who stands up for widows" (Psalm 68:5), so the one who does the same becomes like him, a "son of the Most High" (huios Hypsistou). Jesus promises the same title to those who love their enemies and lend expecting nothing: "you will be sons of the Most High" (Luke 6:35). James defines true religion as "to visit orphans and widows in their trouble" (James 1:27). The Hebrew of the second half differs; see the variant on this verse.
orig: ὡς υἱὸς Ὑψίστου (hōs huios Hypsistou)
r: Psalm 68:5; Luke 6:35; Matthew 5:9; Matthew 5:45; James 1:27; Deuteronomy 10:18

a: Wisdom
p: In 4:11–19 Wisdom is a mother and teacher who tests her pupils; in the Hebrew she speaks in her own voice.
b: Here Wisdom acts as a person again, so the Plain gives her a capital W. In the Greek, Ben Sira describes her from outside. In the Hebrew of manuscript A she begins to speak herself from 4:15 on: "Whoever listens to me will judge truth... I will walk with him in disguise." Jesus says, "wisdom is proved right by all her children" (Luke 7:35). Christian readers have heard Christ, the Wisdom of God, in such passages; Jewish readers hear the Torah, which Ben Sira himself identifies with Wisdom (24:23). The Catholic lectionary reads 4:11–19 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time.

a: sacred service for the Holy One
p: The Greek verbs are temple words: those who serve Wisdom are like priests serving the Holy One.
b: Latreuontes ("serving, worshiping") and leitourgēsousin ("will do sacred service") are the Greek Bible's words for the work of priests and Levites. Hagiō can mean "the Holy One" or "the holy place," and the Hebrew of manuscript A, "those who serve her are ministers of the holy," is just as open. Ben Sira loved the temple and its priests (7:29–31; 45; 50). Here he makes the service of Wisdom a kind of priesthood.
orig: οἱ λατρεύοντες αὐτῇ λειτουργήσουσιν ἁγίῳ; Hebrew משרתי קדש משרתיה

a: she will put him through torment by her discipline
p: Here paideia is "discipline" in its hard sense: Wisdom tests her pupil with fear and torment before she trusts him.
b: The path to Wisdom begins on "crooked ways" with "fear and terror." Basanizō means to test by torture, as metal is tested on a touchstone. The Plain uses "discipline" for paideia here because the sense is correction and hardship (contrast "instruction," 1:27; 6:18). Proverbs says, "The LORD's discipline, my son, do not reject" (Proverbs 3:11), and Hebrews builds on it: "For whoever the Lord loves, he disciplines" (Hebrews 12:6). Swete's Codex Vaticanus spells the word paidia, a common spelling of paideia in that manuscript.
orig: βασανίσει αὐτὸν ἐν παιδίᾳ αὐτῆς (basanisei auton en paidia autēs)

a: where your own soul is concerned, feel no shame
t: Shame that helps and shame that harms
p: 4:20–26 is a little essay on shame: be ashamed of wrong, but never too ashamed to do right.
b: Greek moral writers praised a healthy sense of shame (aidōs) and warned against false shame that stops a person from doing what is right. Ben Sira teaches both. Do not feel shame for your own soul's good (4:20); some shame "leads a person into sin," some is "honor and grace" (4:21). Do not let respect for great men make you fall (4:22, 27); do not be ashamed to own your sins (4:26). Paul draws a similar line between two kinds of grief (2 Corinthians 7:10). Ben Sira returns to the theme in 41:14–42:8.

a: Do not favor anyone's face
p: The Greek idiom "take a face" means to show favoritism, from a Hebrew phrase "lift a face."
b: Lambanein prosōpon, "to receive a face," renders the Hebrew nasa' panim, "to lift a face," which means to favor someone because of who he is. The law forbids it in court (Leviticus 19:15), and the New Testament makes a noun of it: God shows no prosōpolēmpsia, no favoritism (Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11), and James says, "do not mix favoritism with the faith of Jesus Christ" (James 2:1). Ben Sira's twist is that favoring others can harm "your own soul." The Hebrew has the same idiom: "Do not lift your face against yourself."
orig: μὴ λάβῃς πρόσωπον (mē labēs prosōpon); Hebrew אל תשא פניך
r: Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11; James 2:1; James 2:9; 4:27

a: Never be ashamed of
p: The Greek says "do not be ashamed to confess your sins"; the Hebrew says "do not be ashamed to turn away from sin."
b: Homologēsai means to admit openly, to confess. Jews confess sins to God in the prayers of the Day of Atonement and on other days; the Bible's examples include Leviticus 16:21 and Nehemiah 9:2. The New Testament says, "confess your sins to each other" (James 5:16), and "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and he is just: he will forgive us" (1 John 1:9). Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess to God in the presence of a priest, in the sacrament of confession; most Protestants confess to God directly, sometimes also to a pastor or a fellow believer. The Hebrew of manuscript A has a different verb (see the variant).
r: Leviticus 16:21; Nehemiah 9:2; Psalm 32:5; Proverbs 28:13; James 5:16; 1 John 1:9

a: the Lord God will go to war on your side
t: God fights for the one who fights for truth
p: If you struggle for what is right even to death, God himself will fight for you, as he did for Israel at the sea.
b: Agōnizomai is an athlete's or fighter's word: "contend, struggle." The promise takes up Moses' words at the Red Sea: "The LORD will fight for you" (Exodus 14:14; Deuteronomy 1:30). Ben Sira applies Israel's war language to one person's stand for truth, even "right up to death." The Maccabean martyrs, a generation after him, would take such words literally (2 Maccabees 7).
orig: ἕως τοῦ θανάτου ἀγώνισαι (heōs tou thanatou agōnisai)

a: In your own house
p: Ben Sira's pupils would head households with servants and slaves; he warns them against being tyrants at home.
b: A household then included wife, children, servants and slaves, all under the master's authority. Phantasiokopōn may mean "imagining things" (suspicious, fearful of plots) or "putting on a show" (playing the great man); the Plain takes the first. The New Testament household rules ask the same restraint of masters (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1). The Hebrew of manuscript A has "like a dog" instead of "like a lion" (see the variant).
orig: φαντασιοκοπῶν (phantasiokopōn)

a: Do not keep your hand stretched out for taking
t: Open to take, shut to give
p: The Didache, an early Christian manual, repeats this saying almost word for word.
b: The picture is vivid: a hand open to receive and closed when it is time to give back. The Didache, a Christian manual of about the late first century, has the same image: "Be not one who stretches out his hands to receive, but shuts them when it comes to giving" (Didache 4:5, Lake's translation). Paul quotes a saying of Jesus, "Giving is more blessed than receiving" (Acts 20:35). Where the Greek has "paying back," the Hebrew of manuscript A has "giving": "closed when it comes to giving a gift."

a: Do not rest your weight on your possessions
p: Do not lean on money; Jesus' parable of the rich fool makes the same warning.
b: The rich man who thinks he is secure is a favorite target of the wisdom books: "The one who leans on his riches, he is the one who falls" (Proverbs 11:28; compare Psalm 49:6; 52:7). Jesus told of a rich man who said to himself, "Soul, you have lots of good things stored up, enough for many years" (Luke 12:19), and died that night. Ben Sira tells a similar story in 11:18–19. The Catholic lectionary reads 5:1–8 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time.

a: For the Lord is long-suffering
p: God's slowness to punish is not approval; Ecclesiastes and Paul say the same.
b: Ben Sira imagines a man who sins, sees nothing happen, and decides it does not matter. "Since the ruling on an evil deed is not carried out quickly, the hearts of human beings are full and ready to do evil" (Ecclesiastes 8:11). Paul turns the thought around: "Do you not realize that God's kindness is leading you to repentance?" (Romans 2:4). Makrothymos, "long-suffering," is the Greek Bible's word for God's being "slow to anger" (Exodus 34:6). The Hebrew of manuscript A reads "for God is slow to anger."
orig: ὁ γὰρ κύριός ἐστιν μακρόθυμος (ho gar kyrios estin makrothymos)

a: Do not grow fearless about atonement
p: The Greek has "atonement"; the Hebrew has selichah, "forgiveness": do not count on it while you keep sinning.
b: Exilasmos is "atonement," the covering of sin. Manuscript A reads "Do not trust in forgiveness (selichah), so as to add sin upon sin." Ben Sira's warning is the one Paul answers in Romans 6:1: "Should we stay in sin so that grace may multiply?" Both say no. Ben Sira's reason is that mercy and anger are both with God (5:6); Paul's is that those baptized into Christ have died to sin (Romans 6:2–4).
orig: περὶ ἐξιλασμοῦ μὴ ἄφοβος γίνου; Hebrew אל סליחה אל תבטח

a: For mercy and anger are both with him
p: God is not only merciful; his anger at sin is real. Both belong to him.
b: The proverb sets two truths side by side, as Exodus 34:6–7 does: God is compassionate and forgives, yet "by no means clears the guilty." Paul says, "consider God's kindness and God's severity" (Romans 11:22). Ben Sira returns to the pair in 16:11–12. Readers who want only one side, a God of anger or a God who overlooks everything, find no support here. The Plain keeps "anger" for orgē and "fury" for thymos, as in Romans.

a: Do not hold off from turning to the Lord
p: Turn to the Lord now, not tomorrow; the Latin of this line became a classic text on conversion.
b: Epistrepsai, "to turn," renders the Hebrew shuv, the Bible's word for repentance (manuscript A: "Do not delay to turn to him"). The Latin reads Non tardes converti ad Dominum, "Delay not to be converted to the Lord" (Vulgate 5:8, Douay), and the Catholic lectionary heads its reading of 5:1–8 "Delay not your conversion to the Lord." Hebrews urges believers to encourage each other "for as long as the word 'Today' is still being spoken" (Hebrews 3:13), and Paul says, "now is the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2).

a: money gotten by wrong
p: The Hebrew calls it "false riches"; Jesus speaks of "the wealth of dishonesty."
b: The Greek chrēmasin adikois is "unjust money"; manuscript A has nikhsei sheqer, "riches of falsehood," wealth that lies about its value as well as wealth got by lying. It "will not help" on the day of disaster: "Treasures won by wickedness are no help" (Proverbs 10:2; compare Proverbs 11:4). Jesus' phrase "the wealth of dishonesty" (Luke 16:9) is close to Ben Sira's.
orig: ἐπὶ χρήμασιν ἀδίκοις; Hebrew נכסי שקר

a: Do not winnow your grain in every wind
p: A farmer winnows when the wind is right; the man who speaks to suit every wind is "double-tongued."
b: To winnow, a farmer tossed threshed grain into the air so the wind would carry off the chaff. He chose his wind; turning with every breeze would scatter the grain. Ben Sira's picture is of a man who says whatever the moment wants. The diglōssos, "double-tongued" man, says one thing to one person and the opposite to another (compare 1 Timothy 3:8, where deacons "should not say one thing to one person and another to the next"). Ephesians 4:14 warns against being "carried around by every wind of teaching." The Plain renders the refrain in 5:9 and 6:1 the same way.
orig: ὁ ἁμαρτωλὸς ὁ δίγλωσσος (ho hamartōlos ho diglōssos)

a: let what you say be one thing
p: Mean what you say: Jesus' "Yes, yes" or "No, no" makes the same demand.
b: Literally, "let your word be one." The opposite of the double-tongued man is the one whose word is single and steady. Jesus said, "When you speak, say 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no'" (Matthew 5:37), and James, "Let your 'Yes' mean yes and your 'No' mean no" (James 5:12).

a: Be swift when it comes to listening
p: James 1:19 gives the same advice in nearly the same order: quick to hear, slow to speak.
b: "Let every person be ready to listen, slow to talk, slow to anger" (James 1:19). Ben Sira's line uses the same adjective for "quick" (tachys) and the same pairing of quick hearing and patient answer. James never names a source, and the advice is common in wisdom writing (Proverbs 18:13; Mishnah Avot 1:15), so the link may be shared tradition rather than quotation. Manuscript A reads "Be quick to listen, and with patience return an answer."

a: keep your hand on your mouth
p: A hand over the mouth was the gesture of silence before someone wiser or greater.
b: Job, faced with God, says, "I lay a hand across my mouth" (Job 40:4), and Proverbs advises the fool who has spoken too soon: "hand to mouth!" (Proverbs 30:32). Ben Sira gives the rule of the classroom and the council: answer if you understand; if not, be silent.

a: a man's own tongue is what makes him fall
t: The tongue that brings a fall
p: Words bring honor or shame; James's warning about the tongue echoes the wisdom tradition.
b: "Death and life are in the tongue's hand" (Proverbs 18:21). Ben Sira returns again and again to speech (5:9–6:1; 19:6–17; 20:1–8; 28:13–26). James says, "And the tongue is a fire" (James 3:6), and "Whoever never trips in what he says is a complete man" (James 3:2). The Hebrew of manuscript A reads "Honor and shame are in the hand of one who speaks rashly, and a person's tongue is his downfall."

a: a gossip
p: Psithyros is a whisperer, one who spreads rumors; Paul lists such people in Romans 1.
b: Psithyros imitates the sound of whispering. Paul lists "whisperers" among the sins of a world that has turned from God ("They whisper behind backs," Romans 1:29). Manuscript A has a different phrase: "Do not be called a two-faced man," literally "a master of two" (ba'al shtayim), the same expression it uses in 6:1 for the Greek "double-tongued."
orig: ψίθυρος (psithyros); Hebrew בעל שתים (ba'al shtayim)

a: In matters great and small
t: A sentence cut by a chapter break
p: The Greek sentence runs on from 5:15 into 6:1; the chapter division falls in the middle of it.
b: The chapter and verse numbers are much later than the text, and here the break falls mid-sentence: "In matters great and small, do not act in ignorance, and do not trade being a friend for being an enemy" (5:15–6:1). The Plain keeps the Greek numbers, as this site does for all of Sirach, and lets the sentence run across. The Hebrew of manuscript A has a different first line; see the variant.

a: torn to pieces like a bull
p: The Greek is hard to make sense of; the Hebrew reads "Do not fall into the hand of your appetite."
b: The Greek says literally "Do not lift yourself up in the counsel of your soul, so that your soul is not torn apart like a bull." It is not clear whether the soul is like a bull that tears, or like a bull that is torn. Manuscript A reads differently: "Do not fall into the hand of your appetite (nafshekha)" (see the variant). There nefesh, the word behind the Greek psychē, means desire or appetite, as it often does in Hebrew. The Plain keeps "soul" for psychē through this part; in 6:2–4 the sense is "your own desires." The next verse continues the picture: the appetite eats its owner's leaves and fruit.
orig: ἵνα μὴ διαρπαγῇ ὡς ταῦρος ἡ ψυχή σου

a: you will leave yourself standing like dry wood
p: Unchecked desire strips a person like a tree eaten bare: no leaves, no fruit, dry wood.
b: The Bible often compares a person to a tree. The righteous is "like a tree set out by channels of water" (Psalm 1:3; Jeremiah 17:8). The one ruled by his appetite eats up his own leaves and fruit until he is "dry wood" (xylon xēron), the same words Jesus used on the way to the cross: "what will happen to the dry?" (Luke 23:31).

a: A sweet voice will multiply a man's friends
p: The section on friendship (6:5–17) opens with speech: pleasant words gather friends.
b: Larynx glykys is literally "a sweet throat." Proverbs agrees: "Kind words are a comb full of honey: / sweet to the soul, medicine for the bones" (Proverbs 16:24), and "A soft-spoken answer turns fury back" (Proverbs 15:1). Paul asks that speech "always come with grace" (Colossians 4:6). The friendship section that follows is one of the best-known passages of Ben Sira; the Catholic lectionary reads 6:5–17 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time.

a: for advice, one out of a thousand
p: The Talmud quotes this in the name of Ben Sira: many may greet you; tell your secret to one in a thousand.
b: The Babylonian Talmud quotes it among sayings of Ben Sira: "Let many be those who seek your peace; reveal your secret to one in a thousand" (Sanhedrin 100b; compare Yevamot 63b, as the Sefaria text gives them). In Sanhedrin 100b the rabbis debate whether Ben Sira may be read at all, and Rav Yosef concludes that its good sayings may be taught. Manuscript A reads "Let the men at peace with you be many, but your confidant one in a thousand." Ecclesiastes has a similar number: "One man out of a thousand I have found" (Ecclesiastes 7:28).
r: Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 100b; Babylonian Talmud Yevamot 63b; Ecclesiastes 7:28; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 20:19

a: There is a friend who is one only in his own season
p: Three lines begin "There is a friend": the fair-weather friend, the friend who turns enemy, the table friend.
b: Ben Sira teaches by lists. The fair-weather friend is a friend "in his own season" (en kairō autou), when it suits him. The second turns to hatred and tells the world about your quarrel. The third shares your table but vanishes in trouble. The first and third end with the same line, which the Plain repeats word for word. Proverbs says, "Someone with lots of friends can be broken by them, / but some who love you hold on tighter than a brother" (Proverbs 18:24). The advice to test a friend first (6:7) uses peirasmos, the same word as the testing that God sends in 2:1.

a: a friend who shares your table
p: Sharing a meal made people friends in the ancient world; betrayal by a table companion was the bitterest kind.
b: To eat together was to be bound in friendship and loyalty. So the Psalms lament, "Even the man I was at peace with, the one I trusted, / who ate my bread, / has raised his heel high against me" (Psalm 41:9), and Jesus applied that verse to Judas at the Last Supper (John 13:18).

a: A faithful friend is a solid roof over you
p: Three lines praise "a faithful friend" (6:14–16); a Qumran copy preserves 6:14–15 in Hebrew.
b: Skepē is shelter or covering: a roof against storms. Proverbs praises the friend who stays: "At every time a friend keeps loving" (Proverbs 17:17). The Bible's great example is David and Jonathan (1 Samuel 18:1–3; 20:17), and Jesus calls his disciples "friends" (John 15:15). A small Hebrew fragment from Qumran Cave 2 (2Q18), copied before AD 68, preserves parts of 6:14–15 and 6:20–31, so these lines were read in Hebrew in Judea within a century or two of Ben Sira. The fragment, like manuscript A, reads "a faithful friend is a mighty friend" in 6:14.

a: those who fear the Lord will find him
t: Friendship and the fear of the Lord
p: Ben Sira grounds friendship in the fear of the Lord: the God-fearing find faithful friends.
b: Greek writers on friendship, such as Aristotle, taught that true friendship is between good people who are alike. Ben Sira adds the fear of the Lord: those who fear him find faithful friends, and their friends become like them (6:17). The Latin adds "and immortality" after "a medicine of life" (Vulgate 6:16, Douay: "the medicine of life and immortality"); the Greek has no such words.

a: from the time you are young
p: A new section (6:18–37) on seeking wisdom begins with youth: learning begun early lasts to old age.
b: "Good for a man: to carry a yoke while he is young" (Lamentations 3:27); "Train a young person according to his way" (Proverbs 22:6). Ben Sira's school was for the young (51:23), and he promises that learning begun early keeps bearing fruit "right up to your gray hairs." Manuscript A lacks this verse; its text runs straight from 6:17 to 6:19.

a: Go to her as a farmer goes to plow and sow
p: Seeking wisdom is like farming: hard work first, then a harvest.
b: Ben Sira's farmer plows, sows, waits and then eats. The work is real but small next to the harvest. The New Testament uses the same picture: "In the proper season we will bring in the harvest, as long as we do not quit" (Galatians 6:9; compare James 5:7; 2 Timothy 2:6). In the Hebrew of manuscript A the farmer is "one who plows and one who reaps," and the harvest comes "tomorrow."

a: A man without sense
p: The Greek "heartless" and the Hebrew "lacking heart" mean a person without sense, Proverbs' "senseless."
b: Akardios, "without a heart," renders the Hebrew chasar lev, "lacking heart," which manuscript A and the Qumran fragment 2Q18 both have. In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought, so the phrase means "without sense." Proverbs' Plain renders it "senseless" (Proverbs 7:7; 9:4). The first line in the Hebrew calls Wisdom "rugged" or "steep" for the stubborn fool ('evil), the same Proverbs word as in Proverbs 1:7.
orig: ἀκάρδιος (akardios); Hebrew חסר לב (chasar lev)

a: a heavy stone for testing strength
p: Young men tested their strength by lifting heavy stones; the fool tries Wisdom once and drops her.
b: A lithos dokimasias, "stone of testing," was a heavy stone used to prove strength. Wisdom feels like such a stone to the senseless man: he heaves her off as soon as he can. Zechariah uses a similar picture of Jerusalem: "a stone too heavy for any of the peoples. All who lift it will tear themselves badly" (Zechariah 12:3). The Hebrew of manuscript A and 2Q18 has "a stone of burden."
orig: λίθος δοκιμασίας ἰσχυρός (lithos dokimasias ischyros)

a: Step into her shackles with your feet
p: Wisdom's shackles, collar and ropes are a yoke: a burden that becomes protection, glory and joy.
b: Ben Sira uses the language of a slave or a work animal: fetters, a neck collar, a load on the shoulder (6:24–25). The surprise comes in 6:29–31: the fetters become a shelter, the collar a robe of glory, the ropes a royal blue. The rabbis spoke of "the yoke of the Torah": "whoever takes upon himself the yoke of the Torah, they remove from him the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly concerns" (Mishnah Avot 3:5, Kulp's translation on Sefaria). Ben Sira himself ends his book, "Bend your neck under the yoke" (51:26). Jesus' invitation uses the same picture of himself (see 6:28).

a: With your whole soul draw near to her
t: With all your soul and strength
p: The words echo the Shema: love God with all your heart, being and strength.
b: "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5). Ben Sira gives the seeker of Wisdom the same whole-hearted command. Manuscript A lacks the verse, but the Qumran fragment 2Q18 has its second line in Hebrew, "and with all your might keep her ways," using me'od, the same word as "strength" in Deuteronomy 6:5.

a: you will come upon her rest
p: At the end of the hard yoke comes rest; Jesus' "my yoke ... rest for your souls" uses the same pattern.
b: Wisdom's yoke leads to anapausis, "rest," and turns into gladness. Jesus' invitation follows the same pattern: "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down, and I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28), and "Lift my yoke onto yourselves and learn from me ... And you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29). Read beside Ben Sira, Jesus speaks the way Wisdom speaks to her learners (6:24–31; 51:23–27). The promise of rest also stands in Jeremiah 6:16, "you will find rest for yourselves" (Hebrew "for your souls"), so both may draw on the prophets. Either way, Matthew's first readers would have known this kind of invitation.

a: threads of blue
p: The Hebrew is petil tekhelet, "a cord of blue," the exact words of the law of tassels in Numbers 15:38.
b: Hyakinthinos is the Greek Bible's word for the costly blue-violet dye made from sea snails, used in the tabernacle curtains and the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:31). Manuscript A and the Qumran fragment 2Q18 both read petil tekhelet, "a cord of blue," the very words of Numbers 15:38: "They are to put a cord of blue-violet on the tassel of each corner." So Wisdom's ropes are like the tassels every Israelite wore to remember the commandments (Numbers 15:39): her bonds are the law itself, and they are royal.
orig: κλῶσμα ὑακίνθινον (klōsma hyakinthinon); Hebrew פתיל תכלת (petil tekhelet)

a: you will grow shrewd
p: Panourgos usually means "crafty," but here, as in Proverbs, it is the good shrewdness of the wise.
b: Panourgos (compare 1:6) translates the Hebrew 'arum; manuscript A has the verb te'erom, "you will become shrewd." Proverbs' Plain uses "shrewd" for this word in its good sense (Proverbs 8:5, 12), the skill of seeing danger and acting wisely. The snake of Genesis 3:1 is 'arum too, "shrewder than every wild animal," but in a bad sense.
orig: πανοῦργος ἔσῃ (panourgos esē); Hebrew תערם (te'erom)

a: where the elders are many
p: The young learner is to stand among the elders, cling to the wise and wear out their doorsteps.
b: Ben Sira's picture of learning is personal: find a wise man and attach yourself to him (6:34), go to his door at dawn so often that you wear down the step (6:36). The early rabbis gave the same advice: "let thy house be a house of meeting for the Sages and sit in the very dust of their feet, and drink in their words with thirst" (Mishnah Avot 1:4, Kulp's translation on Sefaria), a saying credited to Yose ben Yoezer, who lived not long after Ben Sira. Manuscript A lacks 6:34.

a: murmur over his commandments at all times
p: The chapter ends where Psalm 1 begins: wisdom comes to the one who murmurs over God's law always.
b: Meleta means "practice, go over, meditate," the Greek of the Hebrew hagah, to murmur aloud in study. Psalm 1 says of the happy man, "he murmurs over his law day and night" (Psalm 1:2), and Joshua was told, "Murmur it to yourself day and night" (Joshua 1:8). Manuscript A has the same verb, "meditate always," but names "the fear of the Most High and his commandments." The section ends as it began (6:18): wisdom is a gift God gives to the one who seeks it.
